evidence_quotes.quote: Destarte, o presente artigo possui como objetivo analisar a política pública de saneamento, com ênfase no serviço de esgotamento sanitário, a partir da observância de três princípios que a orienta (universalização, sustentabilidade econômica, governança), de municípios com sedes inserida nas Bacias Hidrográficas do Leste (BHL), no Estado da Bahia.

Além dos dados secundários adquiridos nestes bancos de dados, foram solicitados dados às prefeituras dos municípios que não possuíam dados ou dados incompletos em esgotamento sanitário na base do SNIS.

Os 13 municípios analisados neste indicador representam 84,54% da população da bacia, com um índice de atendimento de 39,39% em 2017. Isto implica em afirmar que em relação à população de toda a bacia (537.298 habitantes), menos de 50% desses habitantes possuem, ao menos, acesso ao serviço de coleta.

No tocante a governança, com destaque para a existência do Plano Municipal de Saneamento Básico, constata-se na Tabela 2, que apesar da previsão do Plano de Saneamento Básico (PMSB) no art. 9º, I, da Lei 11.445 de 2007, após dez anos de sua promulgação (2017), apenas 15% dos municípios inseridos na Bacia (Itabuna, Santa Luzia e Itajú do Colônia) elaboraram o PMSB.

É importante destacar que para estes municípios que não apresentaram todos os dados utilizados lançados no SNIS, foram enviadas solicitações a partir do sistema E-SIC e SIC, que constituem meios para o cidadão pedir informações públicas aos entes.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines population access to municipal sanitary sewage collection and treatment services across 20 municipalities with headquarters in the East Watersheds (BHL), Bahia, Brazil.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 (yes) but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (no). Under the plain wording, the study empirically examines governance and legal-administrative indicators — specifically municipal adoption of Municipal Basic Sanitation Plans (PMSB) under Law 11.445/2007, per-capita public/provider sanitation investment, and municipal compliance with Brazil's Access to Information Law (Law 12.527/2011) via e-SIC freedom-of-information portals. Under the 2026-10-13 clarification, however, none of these empirically analyzed variables is a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden on service users/applicants, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement/disconnection, or utility ownership/regulatory structure governing access). Instead, PMSB elaboration status and per-capita investment represent macro-governance planning and fiscal delivery background (with PMSB deadlines discussed as conditions for municipalities to receive federal budget transfers), while the e-SIC analysis tests researchers' public-records requests for missing SNIS administrative statistics rather than rules governing household sanitation access. Doctrinal discussion of STJ sewage tariff case law in Section 2 is purely background commentary without empirical analysis.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains descriptive quantitative and qualitative empirical evidence drawing on secondary municipal indicators from SNIS (2016-2017), IBGE MUNIC (2017), and SEI (2017), supplemented by primary Freedom of Information requests filed via e-SIC and physical protocols across 13 municipal governments.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports municipal-level sewage access and service coverage outcomes for 2016-2017, including the population sewage attendance index (Índice de Atendimento, Table 1), sewage collection percentage (SNIS IN015, Figure 1), and sewage treatment percentage (SNIS IN056, Figure 2).
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the unit of analysis and population (20 municipalities headquartered in the East Watersheds, Bahia, totaling 635,546 residents in headquarters in 2017, with subsets of 12 to 20 municipalities per indicator), descriptive governance/investment dimensions, sewage coverage outcomes, and a descriptive cross-sectional quali-quantitative municipal study design, although dimensions are presented descriptively in parallel rather than estimating the effect of an access-governing rule.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in Portuguese, which is directly eligible without translation under Criterion 9.

study_design: Descriptive cross-sectional mixed-methods (quali-quantitative) municipal-level study using secondary administrative data (SNIS, IBGE MUNIC, SEI for 2016-2017) and primary Freedom of Information (e-SIC/physical) requests.
population_and_sample: 20 municipalities with municipal headquarters located in the East Watersheds (Bacias Hidrográficas do Leste - BHL) in Bahia, Brazil (total headquarters population of 635,546 inhabitants in 2017; indicator subsamples of 12, 13, 17, and 20 municipalities in 2016-2017). Unit of analysis: municipality.
exposure: Macro-level municipal sanitation planning, public investment per capita, and public-records transparency (existence of a Municipal Basic Sanitation Plan [PMSB] in 2017, per-capita municipal/state/provider sewage investment in 2016-2017, and municipal e-SIC / Freedom of Information responsiveness to data requests); no rule-type mechanism governing household service access is empirically examined.
outcome: Municipal sanitary sewage coverage and service indicators in 2016-2017: population sewage service attendance rate (Índice de Atendimento), sewage collection index (SNIS IN015), and treated sewage index (SNIS IN056).
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Although the paper empirically describes municipal sewage coverage and collection/treatment rates across 20 municipalities in Bahia (satisfying c1, c3, c4, and c6) alongside "governance" and "investment" indicators (which would qualify under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2), its empirical governance measures consist solely of whether municipalities had drafted a Municipal Basic Sanitation Plan (PMSB), per-capita public infrastructure spending, and whether municipal halls responded to the authors' Freedom of Information (e-SIC) requests for missing SNIS statistics. It does not empirically examine any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community access to sanitation services (such as eligibility rules, tenure or documentation requirements, connection or tariff rules, user-facing administrative burdens, enforcement/disconnection, or utility ownership/regulatory structure governing access).
